semantic_reviews.reconstruction_test: q6_learner_test: OBJ-6116-1.2.3-05 (ITEM-6116-1-041, 5 marks): from 1.2.3 alone, a learner puts temperature on x and time on y, labels them temperature / °C and endpoint time / s, uses regular scales (1, 2, 5 or 10 per square), plots with crosses, draws a smooth curve and titles it 'endpoint time against temperature'. This earns 5/5. OBJ-6116-1.2.5-05 with 1.2.1-04 (ITEM-6116-1-P03, 10 marks): 1.2.1 gives IV setting and DV time; 1.1 gives the mean 60 s; 1.2.3 and 1.2.5 give the trend with quoted values; 1.2.1 and 1.2.6 give the controlled 30 cm³; the 1.2.5 anomaly section gives 55 s as the anomaly; the 1.2.5 and 1.2.6 timing guidance gives too-short times and starting at a defined moment. This earns 10/10. The 6-flashcard sample was not done because the file contained no flashcards. q7_misconceptions: ITEM-6116-1-106-MISCON (MISCON-6116-029) confronts the wrong label, but the stem gives the answer away by using 'changes' and 'measures', so it only partly discriminates (1-002). P01 Q1 tests the same idea and is similarly cued (1-003).

issues.finding: The notes and items give two different eye positions for avoiding parallax when reading a ruler. 1.1 and item 057 say the eye should be directly above the mark, which is correct for a ruler lying flat. 1.2.5 tells learners to "read at eye level" for the same oblique-ruler case, and P01 Q8 keys "Read at eye level" as the general precaution against parallax. "Eye level" is right for a vertical scale (measuring cylinder, thermometer) but not for a ruler on a bench. The real condition, that the line of sight is perpendicular to the scale at the reading point, is never stated.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner learns "eye level" as the rule for parallax and uses it for a horizontal ruler, or sees the two notes as contradicting each other. If 057 were marked strictly, an answer of "read at eye level" taken from 1.2.5 could lose the mark.
issues.recommended_repair: State the rule once with its condition, that the line of sight is perpendicular to the scale at the reading, so the eye is directly above a flat ruler and level with a vertical scale or meniscus. Change "read at eye level" in 1.2.5 to "read with the eye directly above the mark". Reword P01 Q8 option B to "Read with the eye perpendicular to the scale", or set the question on a vertical scale.
issues.resolution: 1.1 notes now state the rule with its condition: line of sight perpendicular to the scale at the reading, eye directly above a flat ruler, level with a vertical scale or meniscus. 1.2.5 'read at eye level' changed to 'read with the eye directly above the mark, so the line of sight is perpendicular to the scale'. P01 Q8 stem now 'when reading a scale' and option B 'Read with the line of sight perpendicular to the scale'; explanation updated. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The misconception item only partly discriminates. The stem already describes salt concentration as the factor the learner "changes" and growth as what the learner "measures", and says the labelling is an error. With the two definitions, the answer is just a relabelling. The learner never has to work out which variable was manipulated from a neutral description, which is the misconception's own discriminating_test.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner who confuses the two variables could still score by matching the verbs "changes" and "measures" to the definitions. The item would then show false mastery of the misconception that examiners reported.
issues.recommended_repair: Describe the investigation neutrally, for example "Seedlings were grown in solutions of 0, 1, 2 and 3 % salt and their height recorded after 7 days", and ask the learner to name the independent and dependent variables, or to judge a learner's claim that height is independent with a reason.
issues.resolution: ITEM 106 MISCON stem rewritten neutrally (seedlings in 0, 1, 2, 3 % salt, height recorded after 7 days); learner claims height is independent and must judge whether that is right. Answer and guidance updated; tariff, subtype and labels unchanged. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The stem of P01 Q1 gives the answer away. It says soaking time is "chosen" and germination is "counted". Options C ("The measured response") and D ("The final percentage") are not variables named in the stem, so they are weak distractors.
issues.educational_consequence: The question tests matching "chosen" to the definition, not telling the variables apart in a described investigation.
issues.recommended_repair: Use a neutral description of the investigation, and make the distractors plausible variables (for example temperature, a controlled variable).
issues.resolution: P01 Q1 now describes the investigation neutrally (soaked 0/2/4/8 h, kept at 25 °C, germination counted after 5 days); distractors are the dependent variable and two controlled variables (temperature, seed variety). (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The syllabus wording says that when a further curve is added, vertical crosses (+) may be used to mark its points. The notes say only "a different point symbol" and never name the vertical cross.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner may not know the expected convention for a second data set.
issues.recommended_repair: Add one sentence saying that points on a second curve may be marked with vertical crosses (+), shown in the key.
issues.resolution: 1.2.3 now says points on a further curve may be marked with vertical crosses (+), shown in the key. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The syllabus calls them "constant variables", but the notes use only "controlled variables" and never give the syllabus term.
issues.educational_consequence: A learner asked in an exam for a "constant variable" may not recognise it as the controlled variable from the notes.
issues.recommended_repair: Write "Controlled (constant) variable" in the key-points table and the first sentence of the section.
issues.resolution: Key-points table row and 1.2.1 sentence now read 'Controlled (constant) variable(s)'. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)

issues.finding: The definition of the power of ten is imprecise. It says the power records "how many decimal places separate that value from the original number". It should say how many places the decimal point moves, and in which direction. The worked examples are correct (4.5 × 10⁵, 4.5 × 10⁻⁴, 3.2 × 10⁻⁵, 640).
issues.educational_consequence: Mild confusion with "decimal places" in the rounding sense. The examples correct it.
issues.recommended_repair: "The power shows how many places the decimal point has moved: positive when the original number is large, negative when it is smaller than 1."
issues.resolution: Standard form definition replaced: the power shows how many places the decimal point has moved, positive for large numbers, negative for numbers smaller than 1. (fixed in the author script and regenerated; checks re-run clean.)
